notes.1a: Generally definitions were satisfactory. Candidates should be advised that where equations are given as definitions then all symbols should be defined.
notes.1b: The great majority of statements did not answer the question that was asked. Candidates needed to read the question carefully and use the variation in the spacing of the molecules to explain the difference in the densities of solids, liquids and gases.
notes.1i: A significant number of candidates obtained the correct answer. The weaker candidates had difficulty with the units and powers of ten.
notes.1ii: Weaker candidates were able to gain partial credit for the equation for pressure. The more able candidates realised that the force required the weight of the slab and that maximum pressure is obtained with the smallest area.
notes.2a: The majority of candidates did not give enough detail in their definition. Candidates should be reminded that a precise definition is needed in order to obtain full credit.
notes.2i: The majority of candidates did not take moments about one point. Candidates should be encouraged to practise questions where there are two unknown forces to be determined.
notes.2ii: A number of candidates were able to gain credit by realising that the resultant force in the vertical direction was zero.
notes.3a: Most answers were correct. Candidates should be encouraged to give some working rather than merely writing down an answer.
notes.3i: The majority of candidates were unable to determine the initial momentum of the ball although the correct value for the horizontal component had been determined in (a)(i). There were very few correct answers for the change in momentum.
notes.3ii: This was generally well answered. Some candidates showed some confusion with conservation of energy, conservation of kinetic energy or conservation of momentum
notes.3iii: Many candidates did not realise that the time to return to the ground was the same as in (ii), the time for the upward journey.
notes.4a: The majority of candidates were unable to explain the difference between the two types of potential energy. It was expected that candidates should know that the key elements for the different potential energies were mass and charge.
notes.4b: The derivations often lacked any explanation. Candidates should be encouraged to give solutions with an explanation of the symbols used and a statement between each step.
notes.4i: There were a number of good solutions. A significant number of candidates found difficulty with the calculation involving a percentage.
notes.4ii: Very few candidates obtained the correct answer. Again the efficiency calculation caused difficulty for the majority of candidates. Candidates would benefit from greater emphasis being placed on the application of basic principles to everyday situations.
notes.5a: Many candidates were not able to give an acceptable definition.
notes.5b: Candidates generally gained at least partial credit for giving the defining equation for resistivity or its units.
notes.5i: There were a number of correct answers. Application of a formula caused problems for some candidates.
notes.5ii: Very few candidates were able to give the correct answer. Candidates did not appear to realise the effect on the circuit of adding a resistance with a very large value.
notes.5iii: Well prepared candidates calculated the correct answer.
notes.6a: Well prepared candidates gave the correct definition. A significant number of candidates were unable to give the required definition.
notes.6i: There were very few answers given with the required precision. A common error was to include a vague reference to a limit rather than the point beyond which the object does not return to its original length. Many candidates also omitted the condition of ‘when the force is removed’. A significant minority also confused the elastic limit with the limit of proportionality.
notes.6ii: A significant number of candidates were able to determine the correct value. There were powers of ten errors and misreading of the scales by the weaker candidates.
notes.6iii: A number of candidates were able to obtain the correct value. A significant number of candidates used an inappropriate equation for the work done extending a spring.
notes.6c: This part tested the understanding of the term ‘spring constant’. Very few candidates were able to demonstrate a good understanding and hence correct answers were seldom seen. Candidates would benefit from further experience of solving problems involving spring constants.
notes.7a: The required explanation of an isotope was not well known by a large number of candidates. Candidates must refer to nuclei in their explanation of isotopes.
notes.7i: Very few candidates were able to give the required quantity conserved in a nuclear reaction.
notes.7ii: Well prepared candidates completed the analysis and gained full credit. It was clear that many candidates had not had sufficient practice with these types of reactions.
notes.7c: A common error was to not to include the neutron absorbed by the uranium nucleus.
notes.key_messages: • Many candidates would benefit from taking a moment to consider the numerical answers that they have obtained, especially as regards powers of ten. A quick check on whether an answer is ‘reasonable’ would allow candidates to detect errors in their working. • Candidates should be encouraged not to ‘round off’ answers at intermediate stages of a calculation, as this can lead to inaccurate and inappropriate final answers. use of the approximation g = 10ms–2 should be discouraged.
notes.general_comments: General Comments This multiple choice paper is set on just the AS part of the syllabus and, with 40 questions to be answered within the time limit of an hour, accurate and quick working is essential. Candidates must know that they should not spend too long on any one question. Many questions need written working if candidates are to maintain accuracy. There is plenty of space on the paper and candidates should make use of it. One question, Question 21, was answered correctly by more than 80% of the candidates and four, Questions 29, 30, 33 and 36, were correctly answered by less than 20% of the candidates.
